title: Starz, Verizon Fios Negotiations Stall, As Network May Be Blacked Out Tonight and Both Sides Blame Each Other

body:
Starz could go dark tonight for Verizon Fios subscribers, the network announced Wednesday. The two sides are engaged in an intense licensing negotiation, and with their current deal expiring at midnight ET, there’s a chance it will go dark for subs.

	In a statement, Starz said it “has been negotiating in good faith with Verizon on a distribution agreement” while Verizon, in its own statement, said “it is disappointing that Starz has chosen to publicly signal a potential channel removal while Verizon remains actively engaged in constructive discussions.”
	

	The premium service has actually shifted its business to more of a streaming model in recent years; the company closed the October-December quarter with 12.7 million U.S. streaming subscribers, up 370,000 customers from the previous period, with a total of 17.6 million across all platforms.


	In their statement, Starz warned that Starz channels, Starz On Demand and the Starz app were in danger of going away on Verizon Fios.

	“Starz has been negotiating in good faith with Verizon on a distribution agreement that would ensure our shared customers continue to have uninterrupted access to Starz premium programming,” said Alison Hoffman, president of Starz Networks, said in a statement. “As an independent programmer dedicated to women and underrepresented audiences, Starz is vital to a competitive media marketplace, providing diverse programming alternatives to content from larger conglomerates. Limiting access to Starz would reduce competition and consumer choice. Unless an agreement is reached imminently, our viewers should be prepared for Verizon to remove Starz.”
	

	In response, Verizon said, “It is disappointing that Starz has chosen to publicly signal a potential channel removal while Verizon remains actively engaged in constructive discussions. Using public warnings to create concern among subscribers is an unnecessary pressure tactic.

	Verizon is committed to offering a wide variety of diverse programming across our lineup, while also protecting our viewers from unjustified price increases. Starz is attempting to use public pressure to force higher rates on our customers which would directly drive up monthly bills for the families we serve. Starz channels remain fully accessible today, and we encourage Starz to focus on completing a fair agreement at the negotiating table rather than causing concern for viewers.

title: ‘South Park’ Goes After Billionaires, Data Centers, Anti-Vaxxers and Trump in Phallic-Filled New Episode

body:
In the second episode of “South Park” (or, rather, “South America”) Season 29, an impassioned Butters sets out to rid South Park of “billionaire weenies” — which, as it turns out, are literal penises — when their data centers start getting in the way of him and his favorite thing: Dr. Pimple Popper.

	Because of the data centers being built in his backyard, Butters’ television loses power constantly, thus making him unable to relax to the videos. “And you know why our electricity went out? Because of the goddamn billionaires that are building data centers right in our backyards,” yelled Butters. “All these little weenie billionaires do is suck up all our resources and leave us with nothing.”
	

	Butters’ parents, on the other hand, begin to fight over their child’s anti-billionaire and anti-AI beliefs, which they decide must be the result of the measles vaccine Butters got in order to attend school. “I knew what that vaccination would do to him because I listened to podcasts,” yelled his dad. “But you couldn’t take time out of your precious day to listen to podcasts, could you? And now your son is a libtard.”


	As it turns out, the weenie billionaires in Butters’ backyard are exactly that: weenies. But tensions are rising in their own town as some of the billionaires are being too public, including by appearing on Joe Rogan’s podcast. “Now that we are growing so rapidly, we must be careful,” said the leader of the weenies. “There are so many of us billionaires now; we might be starting to annoy people. That’s why I talked before about the importance of not drawing attention to ourselves.” When Butters calls an exterminator to get rid of the billionaire town and their data center, he explains, “This is some new strain of billionaire. They like to go on podcasts and get into public arguments with Mark Ruffalo.”
	

	As Butters continues to try to rally the town against the billionaires, the weenies must take matters into their own hands by buying the local news media to stabilize their public enemy, “as any good billionaire should.” “But now, can someone tell me who went out and got in a public argument with Macklemore? God damn it, we had it figured out,” said the lead weenie. “I bought the news so we can make us seem nicer, and then some little penis decided Macklemore needed a good talking to… Nobody cares what you think about Macklemore.” (The comment was a jab at Robert Kraft, the billionaire New England Patriots owner who made headlines earlier this month for what amounted to a ban on the rapper from performing at a number of stadiums while on tour with Ed Sheeran.)

	It wouldn’t be an episode of “South Park” without a Trump appearance, and sure enough, the audience got a glimpse of the president at the very end. As he sits down to go to the bathroom (while listening to his own speeches), his very own weenie billionaire flies out of his unzipped pants.

	Following the second episode’s debut, it appears that creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone are going full steam ahead with the “South America” name change, which was announced earlier this month ahead of the Season 29 premiere. (The decision was a comedic jab at Trump’s recent moves to rename locations including Lake Ontario as Lake America, New Mexico as New America and the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.)

	The premiere — the first episode since taking on the name “South America” — hit 4.2 million viewers in three days, Variety previously reported.

title: ‘Scrubs’ Showrunner Dissects Season 2 Premiere: Is Dr. Cox Going to Live, and Will We Finally See J.D. and Elliott’s Kid?
description: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 2 first two episodes of the “Scrubs” revival, which aired Wednesday night on ABC and wi
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 2 first two episodes of the “Scrubs” revival, which aired Wednesday night on ABC and will stream next day on Hulu.

	When ABC’s “Scrubs” returned earlier this year after a nearly 16-year break, fans were quite divided on one major change in character dynamics: J.D. (Zach Braff) and Elliot (Sarah Chalke) had divorced. In Season 1 of “Scrubs” 2.0, J.D. returned to Sacred Heart as chief of medicine, which put him back in the same workplace as his ex.
	

	And that was the point. If Season 1 was about setting up that new dynamic between J.D. and Elliot, Season 2 is about seeing how they’ve adapted to this new reality. And that includes seeing your ex start to date other people. As the Season 2 premiere episode (“My First Time in a While”) opened on Wednesday, J.D. is smitten by Charlie (Rachel Bilson). But is this just a rebound?


	Meanwhile, along with Episode 2 (“My Mentee”), also shown on Wednesday, viewers get an update on Dr. Cox (John C. McGinley) and his autoimmune disease. And we see some cracks continuing to form in Turk (Donald Faison), while J.D. and Elliott adjust to their roles as mentors to the fresh crop of faces — including new arrivals Grant (John Higgins) and Mimi (Keyla Monterroso Mejia). 

	Besides McGinley, other OG cast members making appearances include Carla (Judy Reyes), Jordan (Christa Miller) and The Todd (Robert Maschio). And later in the season, expect to see more from the Janitor (Neil Flynn) and also Elliot’s ex-flame Sean (Scott Foley).

	Variety spoke with “Scrubs” exec producer and showrunner Assem Batra about the premiere episodes’ revelations, and where we go from here — including whether Dr. Cox will be OK, and if J.D. and Elliot’s child Ollie will be seen.
	
	
		You kick off the season digging deep into Dr. Cox’s disease, and how it impacts J.D. and the others. What made you decide to spend so much more time on that?	

	We focused a lot on that because we set up this very sort of dire, serious feeling last season. We wanted to put our audience at ease that we aren’t in any way putting Dr. Cox in such jeopardy that he might not be with us. We feel like it’s a way of making the audience know that he’s always going to be part of this family. When we were reading comments, people were like, “Is he gonna die?” This is a comedy. We don’t want to go that far with it. So part of it was just showing their continued journey to help Dr. Cox stabilize this particular autoimmune disease that we gave him. With the kind of medications they have these days, people can do very well on them. So it’s just a matter of now finding the right treatment.
	
		I mean, people do die on “Scrubs!” So it was within the realm of possibility that something could happen to Dr. Cox.	

	Absolutely, of course. That is always open and in the air, but we just wanted people to at least feel like our family is back together, and we’re not only playing into the jeopardy of that. That’s why we wanted to focus on treating him as opposed to putting him in jeopardy.
	
		How much do we see Dr. Cox throughout the season? Obviously John has his other job in the Bill Lawrenceverse.	

	I know, we would have loved to see him more. But what we could get with his ‘Rooster’ schedule was about four episodes, so that’s about what we’re going to see him for this run.
	
		We also got to see Judy Reyes as Carla in the season opener, but she also has a day job on “High Potential.” I’m sure it’s been a challenge finding ways to get familiar faces back.	

	We have to give a lot of love to our line producer Mike Livanos, because he’s always going back and forth, trying to figure out how. It’s not just the days we get them to shoot, but they have to fly up to Vancouver. So we really can eke out sometimes a very small amount of time for people who are doing more than one project.
	
		Christa also makes an appearance as Dr. Cox’s wife, Jordan, and she too has another job on Bill’s “Shrinking.” It is nice to see you managing to find ways to get folks in, so they’re still part of the universe.	

	Yeah, everybody’s been so kind about giving their time and coming back to do the show, and we thought it would just be a really fun opener to have her reacting to Perry’s illness because we haven’t seen her point of view on it more than her finding out. We saw her find out, but this is her reacting to what happens when somebody you care about that much is so sick.
	
	
		Things seem to be going OK so far with J.D. and Charlie. What are the plans with those two?	

	I always call these post-divorce relationships the “first pancake” relationships because it’s like you make that first pancake, it’s all weird, and not the most beautiful one, and then you try again. It is a little bit his rebound relationship where he’s finding himself again. And like we see in the early episodes, he’s doing too much and overthinking it. He’s almost reverting back to when he was younger. And so, he does stabilize with her a little bit more as we see them together. But this is very much trying to show that first relationship after a big breakup.
	
		And there’s the moment where he hires Joey Fatone to do a Cameo for her.	

	That was going to be an off-screen joke, and then we found out Joey Fatone was OK to come do the joke. So it was great.
	
		How would you describe these first few episodes in terms of storylines that will evolve as the season goes on?	

	We really want to explore who J.D. and Elliot are now that they aren’t together as a couple. What’s their new normal? We don’t have that many episodes to tell the stories of them outside of the hospital, but we do want to see them a little bit as parents and who they are to one another now that they’re back in the friendship zone of post-divorce. 
	
		Are we going to see their child?	

	If I’m allowed to do that as a spoiler, we will. We will see their kid. We don’t have a lot of time, as we’re telling these stories and wanting to get all of our new cast in as well. But where we can sprinkle it in, even if it’s a mention, we try to keep that whole world alive, that they are parents now.
	
		Donald has talked in other interviews about how you’re exploring Turk’s mental health a bit more this season. It was hinted at briefly last year. How will you dive in a little more on that?	

	It’s important for us to not just let it drop. We’re a comedy, and we want to show our relationships and the fun dynamics between friendships. But it is important for us to mention that these things don’t just disappear for people. We do hit on that a little bit, and what is J.D.’s take on it for his friend. 
	
		And then we know Scott Foley is coming back. Can you tease what’s going to be happening with him and with Elliot?	

	What was great was how when he came back in, it just felt like he had never left. It felt like he was such a part of it. What happens when somebody you’ve always had chemistry with, but never could quite work it out, comes back into your life. Do you say? Do you give it another shot? That’s Elliot’s dilemma. She’s in a very different place, and what does that mean for them?
	
	
		Sounds like there’s a lot on J.D. and Elliot handling the fact that they’re both moving on. What does what does that mean for the two of them?	

	They don’t even really know. As we, the writers, explore it, you can see that they’re on their own journey, which is one of the reasons we chose to not have them stay married. We kept Turk and Carla married, but there are so many fun, interesting things to explore with J.D. and Elliot. What’s it like to see your ex date when you’re also working with them, and you have to know everything about their personal life? How does that make you feel? What does it mean to now be a friend again and not a partner. We get to explore all of those very organic things that happen to people after a breakup, and because they’re working together, it’s intensified for them. This season is a little bit more about J.D. and Elliot in those terms of who they are to each other now.
	
		Another story you left hanging last season was the janitor and the janitor’s son, and the renewal of that rivalry.	

	We have a little bit of fun coming up with them and picking up on this sort of bizarre idea that this is the janitor’s son, or is it really? What’s going on with this? It gives Neil a good reason to come back if his son is in the hospital. So we play a little bit of that in an episode as well.
	
		With Joel Kim Booster departing and both Dr. Cox and the Janitor only guest starring, does J.D. need another foil?	

	We have John Higgins as sort of a frustration for J.D. Whereas J.D. was always so needy, wanting Dr. Cox to be his mentor, now he’s still kind of needy, wanting Grant, the character played by John Higgins, to be his mentee. He’s like, “Why don’t you like me more?” That color on J.D. was always so fun — the neediness, and it gives him a way to play that still. Grant may not be a foil in terms of stopping him from accomplishing what he wants in the hospital, but he’s not accomplishing that mentor-mentee relationship that he craves, that he had with Dr. Cox or believes he had. 
	
		Yeah, I noticed there’s already sort of a generational thing going on with the two of them, with JD willing to bend the rules to help Dr. Cox, and Grant saying, absolutely not.	

	It’s funny that you pick up on that, but that is a very Gen Z thing of how they don’t look at things the same way. Something that he learned from Dr. Cox, and we always think of as metaphorical parents, is that you’re going to pass down what you learn, and it’ll be easy. But the interesting thing about so-called parenting or being a mentor, it’s never easy. There’s always something you didn’t see coming. Grant’s personality is so different. He’s an ethical person, but J.D.’s an ethical person too. They just see whatever that means in two different lights. It’s a fun dynamic for us to play with.
	
	
		Elliot is also doing her own mentoring and also seeing those limitations too.	

	And that’s another fun Gen Z thing to play. The thing I love about this generation is, they don’t see age as a limitation the way Gen X was taught to see it. That’s a cool thing to play between Tosh (Ava Bunn) and Elliot, where Tosh is just kind of like, “it’s not too late to do what you’ve always wanted to do.” That’s just like a new thing for Elliot to hear.
	
		I know you’ve been asked a lot about Ken Jenkins returning as Dr. Kelso. Any hope of an appearance?	

	What I tell everybody is, we have to remember that people have their stuff going on in their lives. They can’t always do these things, and it doesn’t mean they don’t want to. It’s just whatever limitations they’re having in their own life or schedule. He knows that the door is always open. He could call me today and say I can fly in next week, and I would write him in. So it’s really just a matter of if he could make it happen, we’re here for him. 
	
		Any other themes you want to tease for this season?	

	There’s mentorship. I think honestly, the J.D./Elliot of it all. I hope our audiences can be excited about that because I think people have questions about why we broke them up. That’s one of those cool relationships where you’ll always wonder why they couldn’t work. But that’s just one of the complex things we get to play between them.

title: Netflix’s Ted Sarandos on If He Sees Paramount-Warner Bros. As Competition, and If He Courted Casey Bloys: ‘We Had a Very Well-Publicized Lunch’

body:
If Ted Sarandos is concerned about any competitive edge that a Paramount/Warner Bros. merger might pose, he’s not showing it. Speaking Wednesday at the Bloomberg Screentime conference, Sarandos was mostly dismissive of any rivalry: “It’s looked on paper so far it’s one and one,” he said, referring to the company’s two streaming services. “So I don’t know if one and one is two, or one and one is one and a half, or one and one is three.”
	

	When asked about rampant rumors that Sarandos had been courting HBO/HBO Max content chairman Casey Bloys for a job or production deal, the exec downplayed it. “He’s a good guy. For some reason, we had a very well-publicized lunch. We have eaten together many times … He’s going to be in a very good position wherever he does. He’s a super talented guy.”


	The news of Bloys’ ascension to take over Paramount+ alongside HBO Max has not officially been announced, but with a judge giving the final sign-off Wednesday to let the merger proceed, the deal — and some of the new structure, including Bloys’ role — is expected to be announced next week.


	Does Sarandos regret Netflix’s bid for Warner Bros. Discovery? “No, I think the plan was solid,” he said. “We won the deal at some point, so we priced it right. At our scale, that was the top price point where I thought we could return value to our shareholders with that asset. Any more than that, I thought we’d be taking into negative territory, even with our scale. The deal itself kind of threw the business narrative off for investors, for the press, for other folks. You have to be willing to put the business narrative at risk for something that’s good for the long term of the business.”
	

	Meanwhile, Sarandos addressed his relationship with Donald Trump — and whether he thinks a federal production tax credit can happen.

	Sarandos defended Trump when it came to this topic: “For everything else you might think, he is a guy who really cares about the entertainment business, and he cares about protecting the industry and creating jobs, and he loves creating jobs in the entertainment business in America,” Sarandos said. “We talk a lot about how that could work and what’s the upside and the downside of that. 

	“We’ve shot in all 50 states, so we understand where it works and where it doesn’t, where these incentives actually do create jobs and where they don’t,” he added. “A good chunk of the production in America has gone to the U.K. because it’s a very big, very attractive incentive. Public companies have a fiduciary responsibility to deliver the most they can for the money, so they chase those incentives all over the place. In the U.S., the states compete with each other for that, but they do not compete well with other countries for it in total. So the federal incentive, which would be a layer of incentive that would go on top of the states’ incentives, would compete with other countries and bring those keep those jobs back in America.”

	Sarandos noted that Netflix has filmed all over the country and has seen where state incentives work best, and he singled out New Jersey as being the most competitive in the country. On the flip side, he warned that California — and Los Angeles in particular — is still not keeping pace.

	“I just think over the years, California got complacent that the talent was here,” he said. “They let the infrastructure age. They make it very difficult to shoot in the city of Los Angeles. I tell you, we just finished the David Fincher’s movie (‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’) and it was no walk in the park.”

	Sarandos opened his conversation by answering questions about Netflix’s slower growth (2% year-over-year growth in user engagement during the first half in 2026). 

	“Yes, overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said. “We are, though, also doing things that create a lot of headwind to that number. Meaning, when we do live programming on Netflix, which is a relatively new thing, we spend about 5% of our content budget on live events. They generate about 1% of our watching.
	

	“We are growing the business,” he added. “We want to keep growing it faster. This past quarter, we did double-digit revenue growth in every region of the world. So the business is great and growing fine.”

	As for adding more content to the service, besides podcasts, he points to the distribution deal Netflix made in France with TF1. “We should be much more nimble to be able to add new ways to watch on Netflix over time,” he said. 

	Also, as Netflix prepares to release “La Bola Negra” in October with the longest theatrical runway in the streamer’s history, Sarandos said they’ll continue to play with windows. Already, Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” next year will become the first Netflix release to receive a conventional theatrical rollout, with a 49-day window preceding its April 2 streaming debut. 

	“So what we’re doing is looking at this model and saying, OK, how do we serve movie lovers who may want to see this movie in a theater, and how do we not harm value to Netflix?” he said. “Last year, we put over 30 movies in the theaters, all with bespoke plans of how many days are going to be out, how much marketing to spend, what cities to play them in. What you figure out is that on one end of the spectrum is ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘Train Dreams’ last year, that could have played in the theaters for six months. Those kind of art house films play like that. And then the other end is the four-quadrant family rewatch movie, so we said, let’s take those two and treat them different. So we’re going to do a big wide release for ‘Narnia’ next year, and we’ll do a big wide release for ‘Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory’ at the end of the year. We think they’ll do great, and when the ‘K-pop Demon Hunters’ sequel comes, you could expect a very broad theatrical release.”

title: Laura Benanti on Her Journey From Broadway to Stand-Up With a Riotous One-Woman Show, ‘Nobody Cares,’ and Why Melania Remains One of Her Proudest Roles
description: Laura Benanti is out of the woods and into a thicket that is very different from her initial Broadway base: the world of stand-up comedy. Officially
body:
Laura Benanti is out of the woods and into a thicket that is very different from her initial Broadway base: the world of stand-up comedy. Officially, “Laura Benanti: Nobody Cares” is a “one-woman show,” but she says the only reason she shies away from calling it stand-up at all is because she respects the people who practice that on a weekly basis too much to want to claim she’s mastered that craft as an interloper. But whatever the comedic equivalent of belting is, that’s a natural skill that Benanti is also turning out to have in her wheelhouse, as she carries the art of quip-riddled personal storytelling as well as she carries a tune.
	

	“Nobody Cares,” which plays at the Wallis in Beverly Hills Thursday through Sunday and moves to Costa Mesa’s South Coast Repertory the following weekend, is not tuneless, so anyone who first came to love Benanti as a Broadway songbird needn’t worry her vocal cords have been clipped for this production. But the handful of songs she works into this current show are all original numbers, conceived in the same mostly irreverent vein as the spoken-word parts that dominate the show. Zero knowledge or prior appreciation is required of her rich history as the breakout starlet powering shows like “The Sound of Music,” “Nine,” “My Fair Lady,” “She Loves Me” and “Into the Woods.” The so-called reformed ingenue is now prepared to tackle middle-aged topics like divorce (in multiples), postpartum depression and the tricky art of balancing self-deprecation and personal pride, via deft writing that suggests maybe she ought to be co-writing her own musical comedies, if she takes a pause  from this confessional vein.
	

	Variety spoke with Benanti about why “Nobody Cares” has been so rewarding for someone who has already received two and a half decades of applause for her stage work… and also, in a peculiar wrinkle, a lot of love (well, from some) for her portrayal of Melania Trump on “Late Night With Stephen Colbert.” The show has been a hit in New York and London, 

	Most people would see “Nobody Cares” and think that you were a very practiced stand-up comedy person, which was never your history prior to conceiving this. it’s been something that was buried latent in you for a long time. Not that this strictly counts as stand-up comedy, but certainly a lot of it is in that sphere or involves those skills.

	Yeah, I would say this show is most akin to stand-up, for sure, and with some good musical comedy in there as well. We have five original songs that I co-wrote with Todd Almond, who’s on stage with me. It’s certainly comedic storytelling. Something I talk about is, I really want people to understand that this is not like a cabaret. This is not Broadway songs or Broadway music in any way. It’s 16-plus (age-wise). There’s adult content; there’s foul language. It’s not what people might expect of me if they only know me from my roles on Broadway.

	Looking at previous interviews you’ve done when you went out with this show, you get those disclaimers in pretty early toward the start of most interviews. You really want to get that message out. That must come from having had a few surprised customers.

	Yeah. I still always have, I’m gonna say, at least 15 people in the audience who are like, “Where am I? Why isn’t she singing ‘The Sound of Music’?” And it does take a little while to win them over, because they don’t want to hear me sing a song about dicks. They’re just like, “What’s going on?”

	Have you had any walkouts over the dicks, and/or the lack of “Into the Woods” content?

	Nobody has left. Well, at least that I could see. Maybe the people in the back have. But nobody’s left. But they certainly have scowled.

	Presumably the scowlers come around eventually? But not everything is for everybody.

	I mean, even the most reluctant husband or boyfriend who got dragged there, by the end of the show, I do feel like I’ve won them over. And for whatever reason, this makes me really happy. My audiences have been, for the most part, really intergenerational, from teenagers to women in their 20s and 30s and 40s all the way through to people in the audience who are in their 80s, and likely they are the people coming knowing me from Broadway. But everybody seems to really enjoy it, and it’s really nice to see all of those people in one place at the same time laughing at the same things.
	

	You’ve been doing other things where people discover your sense of humor. But the people who know you most for the ingenue characters you talk about having been put it early in your theater career, they wouldn’t have reason to naturally make that leap, like, “I can just tell that lady has a really wicked sense of humor.”

	Right. That’s been sort of an uphill battle. But certainly I think even in the ingénues I’ve played, I’ve always tried to pepper in humor wherever I can find it, and to mine humor at any moment, even if it’s not on the page. I’ve done that since I was 18, playing Maria in “The Sound of Music.” That was always a big goal of mine. But I do think that the repertoire certainly that I had till I was 30 was for the most part ingénues. But I think “Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown,” even though that closed early and wasn’t a big hit, educated a lot of people in the Broadway community to the fact that I’m a clown. And I always have been. I’m sort of like a clown that was in an ingenue leading lady’s body.

	And I think doing Melania really helped with that. People realized that I could do sketch comedy and impressions. But I know I’m not the only performer who feels that you just have to sort of keep showing people who you are. Because if you do a lot of different things, like musicals and plays and comedy and drama… it’s harder for people to put you in a box of, this is what you do… I constantly have people be like, “I didn’t know you were funny.” It used to piss me off, and now I’m like, “Yeah, you didn’t, and it’s my job to show you that I am.”

	This show came about from Audible asking you to write and perform an autobiographical piece. So did wanting to do something like this come out of that assignment, or were you always like, “Someday I’m gonna put my own voice out there, whether it’s with a comic sensibility or something else, where I will be as great being myself as I’ve been being an interpreter as I’ve been of other people’s voices”?

	Well, you know, I’ve done these Broadway concerts since I was 22, all over the country, where I would go to wherever and sing Broadway music and then do stories in-between. And the feedback I would often get is people saying, “I loved the stand-up. The stand-up was actually my favorite part.” But I think I was always just too scared to do that outside of the context of the career I had already had — the safety of singing songs that people expect of me. Then I started hosting a bunch of (events) and writing the monologues and and a lot of the bits, and it was so fun. I love the puzzle of a joke. Especially if it’s something that is a serious topic, I love figuring out how to talk about it in a way that makes people laugh and disarm them. So when Audible reached out to me about commissioning a show, I immediately said yes, because I had already been wanting to do that. But then as I started writing it, I just kept thinking, “Nobody cares. Nobody cares what a middle-aged white lady has to say. This is not the voice that we’re clamoring for.” But they paid me, so I had to keep writing.
	

	And slowly, I allowed myself to feel the joy of the puzzle. And I have some really wonderful girlfriends who would come to my makeshift garage and listen to me do jokes and give feedback. And they were like, “I need to hear this, actually. You can be as self-deprecating and as insecure as you want, but what you’re saying is something I actually really need and want to hear, even outside of my friendship with you.” So that gave me courage and solace as I continued to write it. Now that I’m touring with it, I’m seeing that, and that’s still the feedback that I’m getting from audiences, which is really, really gratifying.

	You know what’s so weird is, before X was X, when it was just Twitter and it was fun instead of just the dumpster fire of misogyny that it is now, I really got into it, because the puzzle of having to deliver a joke in 140 characters was really fun for me. I do think that’s where a lot of people started to realize I was funny. I noticed a lot of comics started following me, and I started having back-and-forth bantering with them. People who did not know anything about me at all started following me on Twitter. In some ways, that helped me more than anything, weirdly. And now, I get to do it.

	And I still feel self-conscious about calling it stand-up because I have so much respect for stand-ups, that they have such a hard job. They work so hard, and I do sometimes worry that they’re gonna be like, “Oh, OK, Miss Broadway, Miss ‘I’ve never played a small club.’ You’re a stand-up comic. OK.” But I don’t know how better to describe what I’m doing than that, especially when I’m trying to set expectations for the audience of what it is.

	Were you ever tempted to work more inside-baseball theater stories into the show? Because in interviews you have some hilarious stories about old-timers you’ve worked with and stuff like that. But that’s not the theme of this show. This is about pretty common experiences, or at least exaggerated versions of experiences that have actually happened to you. So you’re talking about perimenopause when you could be sharing theater anecdotes. But you’ve prioritized the most universal stuff.

	Yeah. My intention with this show is to broaden my audience. Of course I want to keep my core musical theater fans; I owe my career to them. But I want to broaden my fan base, and the thing I always say is, you don’t have to know anything about Broadway. You don’t have to like Broadway. One of the lines in my show is, “I want to give a very special welcome to those of you who were dragged here by someone who said, ‘I know you don’t like Broadway, but I think you’ll like her.'” And so my goal with this show is to use it as almost a Trojan horse of, “Hey, everybody, this is what I’m capable of…” And when I do my more Broadway-style concerts, I definitely have theater anecdotes because that’s what that audience really wants to hear. But for me, I want this to be more universal, and not that I’m an actress doing a comedy show. I’m a person telling you stories about my life — which, unfortunately, are not actually that exaggerated. The stories you hear in my show, sadly, are true.
	

	There are moments in the show where you’re very deadpan about how you do the lead-in to the punchline, and the punchline is you delivering the really terrible thing that happened to you, or the shocking secret. And there’s a great comic rhythm to it, even though what you’re talking about is not inherently funny. You’ve actually said that a lot of this is about the worst experiences of your life. Did you have any questions with yourself about whether to go sort of full vulnerability as far as dealing with everything — from beimg twice divorced and making the third time the charm, to breaking your neck, perimenopause and postpartum depression? The lightheartedness of it doesn’t really stop, even though you’re getting into heavy material.

	You know, that’s like my mom coming through…

	Whose approach to finding levity in everything you have talked about. You once described your mother’s approach to finding laughter in the worst circumstances as “giggles at a funeral.”

	And I will say that a lot of these stories have the benefit of hindsight. At the time they weren’t funny, but in retrospect they are. I think that challenging topics feel more accessible to people when they’re laughing, and can make a greater impact, because laughter opens our hearts, and then once a heart is open, you can sort of slip in the message.

	But, like when I was in London, I definitely felt this sense of how my open-hearted, “I wear my heart on my sleeve” (attitude), especially as it pertains to my children, was not as welcome as it is in the States. Which was interesting to feel. There’s a song on my show called “Mama’s a Liar.” The first two sections of the song are comedic, and then the last one is very genuine. And I could almost feel people’s discomfort in London, that during a comedy show I’m singing something emotional. But in the States it’s people’s favorite song. So it’s been interesting to me to see who is ready, willing and able to go on a journey with a comedy show that occasionally has some heartfelt moments. You know, Mike Birbiglia does that in such a masterful way. One of the reasons why I’m such a big fan of his is not only am I laughing, but he’s making me feel something and think about things.

	Do you have a final feeling you want to leave people with, when they come out?
	

	Hmm. I’ve spent a lot of my time feeling a lot of shame about the stories I talk about — and what a waste of time. So I want to make them laugh, and I want them to walk away being like, “Yeah, I’m fine.”

	Let’s talk about your Melania Trump, which oddly enough is something through which a lot of people have learned about you for the first time. Will you find a place to do it again, or was that specific to the Colbert show?

	I mean, it’s so synonymous, (so) I do it a little bit in my theater concerts. I do a medley, as her. And I’ve done it a bit on my Instagram, but I’m not sure where else I would do it, you know? I’m not sure where I’d go with it.

	MAGA was kind of mad at you…

	Uh, yeah.

	But at the same time, you got a huge aount of very positive response for doing that. So how did that work out for you, with this whole world applauding you for this, and then knowing people are pissed off too? Because a big component of the show you’re doing now is that you have always been a people pleaser.

	Exactly. I was just gonna say that, the people-pleasing thing. And then I was like, “You know what? Fine. I don’t want these people to feel comfortable with me.” You know, I had some followers be like, “Stick to singing. I liked you, now I don’t.” And I’m like, “I’m sorry I ever made this a safe space for you. Goodbye.” So I do not shy away from my belief system. If that loses me followers, if that loses me fans, I feel like I’m on the right side of history. But it certainly was scary at times. But that’s for the most part died down. And look, it makes me practice what I preach in this show, which is: Not everybody’s gonna love you, and that’s fine.

	That recurring bit helped set up for people that you have these comedic chops, and you might be exercising them, with a comic sensibility that might be off the beaten track.

	Exactly. And for the people who know me, or have a preconceived notion of who I am, my hope is that they open themselves to this version of me that’s the real part of me. And I hope that people who don’t know me at all will come and enjoy themselves, and I can introduce myself to them as the person I’ve always been. You know, as the recovering ingenue, not the ingenue.

	I may be a little strange, but I’m watching the show and thinking, “Oh, I liked her opm Broadway, but she’s so good at this. She should just do this. She should just do comedy all the time.”
	

	I’d love to do that!

	WIll you continue touring this show into next year and beyond?

	Yeah. But we did film it, in London, and so my hope is that we’ll be able to get a distributor for it, and it’ll be out in the world in some capacity. And frankly, like, I would like to do this forever. I love theater — I’ll always do theater — but my goal with this show is to show people that I’m funny, and especially in L.A., get [00:27:00] people to hire me for comedy. My absolute dream is to be on a television comedy and just get to go to work and laugh all the time, and continue to write more of these shows and tour them. I really love it. It brings me the most joy of anything I do.

	Any quick synopsis of what else is happening in your professional life? You’ve done so much television.

	I’m on “Mayor of Kingstown,” which is coming back; I’m not sure when. But I am a free agent, so anyone who would like to hire me is welcome to hire me.

	This would not be the first time that pronouncement has been made in Variety.

	Yes, please. Exactly. “Dear Hollywood.”

	“Laura Benanti: Nobody Cares” will be performed five times at the Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts, located at 9390 N. Santa Monica Blvd. in Beverly Hills: Thursday, Friday and Saturday nights at 7:30 p.m., and Saturday and Sunday afternoons at 2 p.m. Tickets and other information can found online at thewallis.org or 310-746-4000. Following the Beverly Hills engagement, Benanti will also perform at Orange County’s South Coast Repertory from Oct. 8-11. Tickets for that run are available at scr.org.

schema.headline: Laura Benanti on Her Journey From Broadway to Stand-Up With a Riotous One-Woman Show, ‘Nobody Cares,’ and Why Melania Remains One of Her Proudest Roles

title: Bradley Whitford on Bringing Back ‘The West Wing’ as a ‘Limited Series’

body:
Bradley Whitford is ready to return to the White House.

	The actor tells me that it may be time to bring back “The West Wing” as a “limited series of some kind.”

	Series creator Aaron Sorkin has had fans chomping at the bit ever since he told Variety’s Michael Schneider he was inspired to write more episodes while attending a 25th anniversary of the show at the White House in 2024. “I just got a couple of ideas for episodes just walking around the White House,” Sorkin said at the time. “Like, ‘why didn’t we ever do this? Why didn’t we ever do that?’”
	

	Whitford inspired a “West Wing” reunion earlier today when his fellow castmates Martin Sheen, Dulé Hill, Mary McCormack and Josh Malina joined him at the unveiling of his star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.


	“I’ll work him, I’ll work him,” Whitford said of trying to get Sorkin to commit.


	Hill said the cast wouldn’t hesitate if Sorkin decides to write a new season. “I always say that’s a question for Aaron Sorkin,” he said when asked about a revival. “If he writes it, then I will come. I think if he writes it, then we all will be there.”

	However, Hill continued, “Sometimes I wonder though where things are in the world. Things are so outlandish, I don’t know how you dramatize any of that. With him writing, it would be a lovely thing to hopefully steer the collective consciousness of our society back toward humanity and connectivity and understanding.”

Dulé Hill says the “West Wing” cast is ready to return if Aaron Sorkin decides to write a new season: “We all will be there.”via Bradley Whitford’s Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony pic.twitter.com/xde3oQceuY— Variety (@Variety) September 30, 2026


	“The West Wing” premiered on NBC in 1999 and ran for seven seasons before ending in 2006. The ensemble also included Rob Lowe, Allison Janney, Richard Schiff, John Spencer, Janel Moloney and Stockard Channing.
	

	The series won 27 Emmy Awards from 95 nominations.

title: Mark Ruffalo Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Stifle Creativity’ and ‘Weaken Free Speech’: It ‘Should Never Have Been Approved’

body:
Mark Ruffalo is speaking out against the Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger once again, this time following the news on Wednesday that the deal has been approved and is tentatively set to close next week.

	“This merger will stifle creativity, weaken free speech, and cost people their jobs — it is a bad deal for this country and should never have been approved,” wrote Ruffalo in a statement posted to Threads on Wednesday. “This is an incredibly disappointing outcome for the hundreds of thousands of us who stood up to block it, but it’s also not the end. This grassroots movement isn’t going to fade away and neither is our resolve.”
	

	He continued: “This was never about just one merger: this was about fighting back against corrupt oligarch billionaires trampling the interests of everyday people to line their own pockets. We’re still in that fight. Join us.”


	Ruffalo has long been outspoken about his opposition to the merger. Earlier this month, Ruffalo encouraged California Attorney General Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs not to settle their lawsuit against Paramount Skydance, which would effectively keep David Ellison from acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery.

	“Don’t you dare, [Rob Bonta], do not cave,” Ruffalo wrote on X. “5,670 filmmakers put their necks on the line for you to fight this merger. Another 75,000+ and counting have signed to tell you not to concede in just 3 weeks. You work for the people — the very people who will be hurt if you let this lousy deal filled with empty promises go forward. Please sign to send a message to the AGs and Paramount. Reject the deal. The people don’t want it!”

title: Satyajit Ray Film by Srijit Mukherji, New Feluda and Eken Mysteries Lead Bengali Streamer Hoichoi’s 10th Anniversary Slate
description: A Satyajit Ray film from Srijit Mukherji heads a lineup of more than 25 series, films and TV titles that Bengali streamer Hoichoi has set for its 10
body:
A Satyajit Ray film from Srijit Mukherji heads a lineup of more than 25 series, films and TV titles that Bengali streamer Hoichoi has set for its 10th year. The slate also brings new cases for detectives Feluda and Eken Babu and the platform’s first animated series.

	In “Maharaja Tomare Selam,” Ray agrees to his son’s request to make a children’s film. He then battles money trouble, resistance from the industry and the pressure of his own reputation on the road to what would become a classic of Indian cinema, “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne.” Jeetu Kamal, Ritwik Bhowmik, Rudranil Ghosh, Sairity Banerjee, Shatakshy Nandy and Arijit Dutta star.
	

	The Hoichoi Studio film lineup also includes “The Eken: Kerala-e Kurukshetra,” directed by Joydeep Mukherjee. In it, a botched secret mission drags Eken Babu into a mystery in Kerala. Anirban Chakrabarti, Ritwick Chakraborty, Raima Sen, Somak Ghosh, Suhotra Mukhopadhyay, Ambarish Bhattacharya, Arna Mukhopadhyay, Subrat Dutta and Kamaleswar Mukherjee make up the cast.


	Parambrata Chatterjee directs and appears in “Jononi,” about a college professor who goes looking for her housekeeper’s missing teenage daughter and finds secrets closer to home. Koel Mallick, Koneenica Banerjee and Joy Sengupta also star. Debaloy Bhattacharya’s “Bhugun,” starring Abhishek Banerjee and Parno Mittra, follows a wealthy Bengali family whose deal with a tantric to restore its fortune brings down a deadly curse.

	On the series side, Kamaleswar Mukherjee directs “Feludar Goyendagiri: Baksho Rawhoshyo,” in which Feluda chases the secret of a box swapped during a train journey. Tota Roy Choudhury, Kalpan Mitra and Subhadip Chakrabarti star. Other returning franchises include “Birangana 2,” “Kuheli 2,” “Thakumar Jhuli 2,” “Tansener Tanpura: Mohonbashi” with Vikram Chatterjee, and “Choddobeshi 2,” created by and starring Parambrata Chatterjee. He also directs “Agambagish: Drolmar Khorgo,” starring Saswata Chatterjee. In it, the tantric saint Krishnananda Agambagish takes on a band of ghostly dacoits in 17th-century Bengal.
	

	New series include Pratim D. Gupta’s “Chaalchitro: The Ekchala Murders,” about a serial killer who leaves female victims posed as goddesses in the run-up to Durga Puja. It stars Tota Roy Choudhury, Anirban Chakrabarti, Chanchal Chowdhury and Sweta Mishra. Raima Sen leads “Kumari,” created by Sahana Dutta. Ayan Chakraborti’s “Shrimoti Not Out,” starring Ananya Chatterjee and Joy Sengupta, follows a 48-year-old woman who learns she is pregnant just as her son is about to marry. Mimi Chakraborty headlines Aditi Roy’s “Uttoron: Charulata,” and Sabyasachi Chowdhury stars in “Detective Tarinicharan,” a murder mystery set in colonial Darjeeling.

	Rounding out the series slate are “Debipokkho,” “Kauriburir Mandir,” “Mangolik,” “Konya,” “Shoti,” “Jujuma” and “Kanamachhi.” Sanglap Bhowmick directs the animated “Shri Ramkrishna,” which traces the life of spiritual master Ramakrishna Paramahansa. On TV, Madhumita Sarcar and Arjun Chakrabarty star in “Katha-Amrito,” and Trina Saha stars in “Sholaka Rawhoshyo.” The streamer is also continuing to back Bangladeshi creators and productions.

	“For me, 10 years of Hoichoi is not just about the number of shows we have made or the milestones we have crossed. It is about the stories, characters and creators that have stayed with people and, in many ways, become part of Bengali popular culture,” said Soumya Mukherjee, COO of Hoichoi. “When we started, the ambition was simply to create a home for Bengali stories. Ten years later, that belief remains the same, but the possibilities around those stories have become much bigger. We have seen Bengali IP grow beyond the screen it was created for, through adaptations, licensing, theatrical, partnerships, new formats and, increasingly, our stories are traveling beyond Bengal and beyond language.”

	Hoichoi’s library now holds more than 600 Bengali films and over 200 original series, watched in India, Bangladesh and overseas. Beyond subscriptions, it makes money from licensing, branded content, theatrical releases and distribution deals. It has also moved onto technology it built itself. 

	Newer bets include Hoichoi FM, which carries original audio fiction inside the app, and Sooper, a microdrama venture working across languages and markets. The company is also testing AI tools for development and production through LoglineAI.
	

	Vishnu Mohta, co-founder of Hoichoi and LoglineAI, said the first decade had been about proving a language-first platform could build a meaningful global business. “The next decade is about expanding what that platform can become,” Mohta said. “Technology, AI and new formats are opening up possibilities that simply didn’t exist when we started. Our ambition is to use those possibilities without losing the cultural instinct and storytelling sensibility that made Hoichoi what it is.”

title: Golden Globes Predictions: Let the Genre Games Begin for ‘Obsession,’ ‘Michael,’ ‘Wildwood’ and More
description: Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predi
body:
Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change in response to buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

					Zendaya in “Dune Part Three”
									Warner Bros.
	




	Golden Globes Predictions Commentary (Updated: Sept. 30, 2026): The Golden Globes submission deadline is coming up on Oct. 30, the night before Halloween. Fitting, since for the next 30 days, studios get to decide what costume their movies should wear for the early phase of awards season.

	The Globes split their top film prize into two genres, drama and comedy/musical and the line between them has always been drawn by strategy as much as tone. Remember, this is the same awards show that “The Martian” once won best comedy.

	For the third year in a row, the comedy/musical side looks more competitive than its drama counterpart. We’re used to seeing it the other way around, and several major players still haven’t declared.

	On the drama side, Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” and “La Bola Negra,” the acclaimed epic from Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (better known as Los Javis), lead the early pack. The Netflix title picked up the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, four months after the duo won best director at Cannes. That bodes well for its run.

	The race is still waiting on first reviews for a couple of contenders in the wings. Sources tell Variety that Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three” held its first intimate, small-group screenings this past week. Early word is very positive.

	And on Friday, the New York Film Festival unveils Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” as its centerpiece selection, with Pedro Pascal as a former child prodigy cellist. Searchlight releases it Dec. 4, and it could make for an interesting addition to the race.

	No studio has a trickier sorting job than Amazon MGM Studios this year. It holds three contenders that could all plausibly claim the drama side: Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s “Project Hail Mary” with Ryan Gosling, Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” which finished first runner-up for TIFF’s People’s Choice Award and Bassam Tariq’s critically acclaimed “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” the Orion Pictures release starring Mahershala Ali as a devout hitman.

	“Your Mother” is all but certain to run in drama. So expect at least one of the other two to go the comedy route, if only to keep the studio from splitting its own vote. Our bet is “Hail Mary” goes comedy, and “Rocky” goes drama.

	Focus Features has a choice to make with “Obsession,” Curry Barker’s micro-budget possession thriller that has grossed more than $400 million worldwide. If the studio follows the “Get Out” (2017) and “The Substance” (2024) playbooks, many expect a comedy push. But assess the landscape, especially for breakout star Inde Navarrette, who looks primed for a best actress Oscar nom as a possessed young woman and this pundit starts to wonder — wouldn’t a drama run make more sense?

	“Obsession” will likely find recognition in cinematic and box office achievement, and Navarrette should be nominated on either side of the house. Its best picture prospects face far steeper hurdles. I think the real question is where can she win?



	

					Sandra Hüller in “Fatherland” and “Rose”
									Mubi
	



	Drama actress is less stacked than usual. The only presumed threat to win is Sandra Hüller, who arrives with a double dose of Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” and Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose,” which earned her the best leading performance prize in Berlin. On the comedy side, most pundits and analysts see the trophy as preordained for Julianne Moore’s towering work in Jesse Eisenberg’s beloved “The Debut.” Navarrette would also have to contend with Olivia Wilde in “The Invite,” a film poised to be a big player across the board.

	A drama win would position the 25-year-old Latina breakout as the alternative to Moore, and recent history shows what that moment can do. In each of the past two years, a Globes lead drama winner was someone the Actor Awards (formerly SAG) had passed over: Fernanda Torres for “I’m Still Here” and Wagner Moura for “The Secret Agent.” Both used the win as a springboard into nomination voting and landed Oscar noms. SAG voters have long been resistant to non-English-language performances. Let Hüller, whose two contenders are both in German, walk away with drama actress and she inherits that narrative. 

	UPDATE: Variety has confirmed that “Obsession” will be submitted as a comedy at the Globes.

	Antoine Fuqua’s “Michael,” starring Jaafar Jackson and the first biopic ever to cross $1 billion worldwide, is also awaiting an official decision and it can go either way based on Globes history. “Bohemian Rhapsody” (2018) and Baz Luhrmann’s “Elvis” (2022) were embraced as dramas, and both won lead actor there. “Ray” (2004) and “Walk the Line” (2005) went comedy/musical and did the same. Among other music-driven films, “A Star Is Born” (2018) found love as a drama, while “Inside Llewyn Davis” (2013) went comedy. There’s no rhyme or reason, so anything can happen. We think a comedy/musical run is ultimately in the cards for “Michael,” alongside a run in cinematic and box office achievement. But again, anything can still happen.

	Speaking of box office, what many may not realize is that films must officially submit for the category. Nothing lands on the ballot automatically, and at the 2025 Globes, Villeneuve’s team opted to keep “Dune: Part Two” out of the box office race and vie only for best picture (drama), where it landed a nomination.

	We’re keeping that in mind for the final chapter. “Dune: Part Three” opens Dec. 18, the same day as Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday” and both will have enough presales to qualify, should their studios choose to enter. The hurdle is the calendar. Motion picture nomination ballots go out to voters Nov. 24 and are due back Dec. 4, and Dec. 2 is the final date for film press conferences and uploads to the Globes’ screening platform. In practical terms, either movie would have to show itself to the several hundred voting journalists more than two weeks before opening day. Based on how Marvel has handled prerelease screenings in the past, I wouldn’t expect “Doomsday” to open its doors that early. “Dune 3” is far more likely to play in those stakes. So in other words, don’t assume anything.

	Another development worth watching for is several studios are taking their animated feature contenders seriously enough to push well beyond that single category.

	Laika is gearing up for a huge push behind Travis Knight’s “Wildwood,” and the stop-motion studio isn’t settling for an animated feature nom. It’s trying to change the conversation around animated movies, which too often get dismissed as “kids’ fare.” At 132 minutes, “Wildwood” is billed as the longest stop-motion feature ever made and it’s Laika’s first PG-13 release. After a Telluride conversation earlier this month with Knight and six-time Oscar-nominated cinematographer Caleb Deschanel, the studio previewed selected scenes at SCAD AnimationFest last week. The film world premieres at the BFI London Film Festival on Oct. 11, then opens AFI Fest as its U.S. premiere on Oct. 21, two days before Fathom Entertainment releases it in theaters. Sources tell Variety that in addition to animated feature, Laika plans to submit “Wildwood” for best picture (drama). The Globes reopened their top categories to animation in 2021, but the three animated films to win a top Globe (“Beauty and the Beast,” “The Lion King” and “Toy Story 2” ) all did it in comedy/musical, long before that. A drama bid is new terrain, but it also sends the message: take animation seriously.

	And Laika does have some Globes history on its side with “Missing Link” pulling off an upset win for animated feature in 2020, coincidentally over “Toy Story 4,” which ultimately won the Oscar.

	“Wildwood” won’t be alone. Independent Film Company’s “Tangles,” Leah Nelson’s hand-drawn adaptation of Sarah Leavitt’s graphic memoir about her mother’s Alzheimer’s, is also expected to vie in drama. The biographical Cannes sensation boasts a powerhouse producing team that includes Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Seth Rogen (destined to be an acting nominee for “The Invite”).

	Every placement will ripple into the lead acting races, which the Globes also split by genre. If “Hail Mary” goes comedy, Gosling heads to the side of the house where he won his only Globe, for “La La Land.” A comedy/musical run for “Michael” gives Jackson’s screen debut a friendlier lane than drama, which is filling up fast.



	

					Robert Pattinson in “Primetime,” “The Odyssey,” “Dune: Part Three” and “The Drama”
									A24 / Universal Pictures / Warner Bros.
	



	Start with Robert Pattinson, who has four movies in theaters this year — “The Drama,” “The Odyssey,” “Primetime” and “Dune: Part Three.” How many noms can he collect? For now, his turn as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen in Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime” looks like his easiest path, in actor (drama), with “The Odyssey” offering another option in supporting actor alongside his co-star John Leguizamo. The front-runners in the actor (drama) category are Andrew Scott, playing the late Ian Charleson in Simon Stone’s “Elsinore” and Pattinson’s “Odyssey” co-star Matt Damon. Behind them, John Turturro (“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York”), Pedro Pascal (“Behemoth!”), Sebastian Stan (“Fjord”) and Anthony Ippolito (“I Play Rocky”) will fight for spots.

	Pattinson isn’t the only big name with more than one ticket to the Hollywood party. Penélope Cruz is also in the hunt with two possible supporting actress bids, for “The Invite” and “La Bola Negra,” plus an actress (drama) play for Florian Zeller’s “Bunker,” opposite her real-life husband, Javier Bardem, who could join her with a drama actor nom of his own.

	Wilde should find enough room for her performance in “The Invite,” in addition to a directing nom for it as well. Perhaps even a third, in supporting actress for “Behemoth!” if it catches on. What a year for her.

	Hüller, meanwhile, can double up in drama actress with “Fatherland” and “Rose,” and she has a path in supporting actress for “Project Hail Mary” (and I guess “Digger?”). Nothing in the Globes rules stops a performer from landing two, three or four noms in the same year.

	We’re also always looking for the Globes picks that come out of nowhere and breathe life into a campaign many had underestimated. Could Gemma Chan or Channing Tatum start supporting runs for Beth de Araújo’s “Josephine?” Could Globes favorite Scarlett Johansson get one going for James Gray’s “Paper Tiger?” And I keep circling Merritt Wever in “Primetime” as a possible nom-morning shocker. It would be well deserved.

	Variety’s predictions in every film category follow below. Not all category placements are confirmed, and all are subject to change.

	The 84th Golden Globe nominations will be announced Monday, Dec. 7, with the ceremony, hosted by Nikki Glaser, set for Sunday, Jan. 10, 2027.

                          Still Alive After Two Attempted Lethal Injections
body:
Christa Pike
                          Still Alive After Two Attempted Lethal Injections
                          Lawyers Say She's 'Snoring'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 30, 2026
                            7:26 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Christa Pike is still alive after 2 attempted lethal injections in Tennessee.
      
    
            Around 8:26 p.m. local time, witnesses said “executioners had injected both syringes of lethal injection chemicals and Pike is still alive and snoring” ... her lawyers said in a federal court filing, according to NBC News.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Pike was scheduled to be put to death Wednesday after the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for Tennessee to carry out her execution ... overturning a last-minute stay from a federal appeals court.
      

            They said Pike “has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat,” and that curtains to the death chamber “have gone down twice.”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we previously reported ... Pike's execution was delayed earlier Wednesday when the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the lethal injection just hours before it was scheduled to take place.
      
    
            The Supreme Court later lifted the stay, allowing Tennessee officials to proceed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Pike's attorneys had fought to spare her life ... arguing that jurors who sentenced her to death were not presented with the full extent of her childhood sexual abuse, trauma and mental-health history.
      
    
            Pike was convicted of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Job Corps student in Knoxville. Pike was 18 when Slemmer was killed.

body:
Christa Pike
                          Execution Back On The Books
                          ... After Supreme Court Loss
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 30, 2026
                            5:31 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 30, 2026
                                6:03 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Tennessee can move forward with convicted murderer Christa Pike's execution, the Supreme Court has ruled.
      
    
            On Wednesday, the court decided to lift the stay of execution that had been ordered just an hour before her lethal injection. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
      
    
            Pike's lawyers were trying to get her sentence changed to life in prison, arguing that her attorneys had failed to present her history of sexual abuse and mental health conditions. That's why her execution was paused just an hour before her scheduled lethal injection.
      

        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            In her dissent, Justice Sotomayor said the decision to vacate the stay "interferes with the Sixth Circuit's routine administrative handling of a capital case and unnecessarily prevents the court from giving due consideration to Pike's claim."
      
    
            She went on to say ... "I see no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of the appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            If executed, Pike would be the first woman in over 200 years to be put to death in the state of Tennessee.
      
    
            She was convicted for the 1995 murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, where she bashed her in the head with a piece of asphalt, carved a pentagram into her chest, and kept a piece of her skull as a trophy ... and ultimately sentenced to death.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Court records say Pike had been sexually abused by her grandmother's boyfriend before she could enter preschool, was raped by a neighbor when she was 11, and again by a stranger when she was 17. She reportedly suffers from bipolar disorder and PTSD.
      
    
            Pike never denied killing Colleen, but her lawyers argued that the jury that sentenced her to death never heard about her history of abuse.

                          I Was Held at Knifepoint at 14 ... The Guy Later Killed Someone Else!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 30, 2026
                            5:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Ben Affleck just revealed a pretty wild story ... saying when he was a teen he was held at knifepoint by another kid ... who eventually went on to kill someone else with a knife.
      
    
            The actor opened up about the scary situation to Kerry Washington on her podcast Wednesday, when she asked him if he'd ever been robbed growing up in Cambridge, MA.
      
    
            Ben recalled ... "I remember I was walking home from high school, I was 14 maybe, and I saw these two kids in like literal hoods on the other side of the street. And, you know, it’s kind of one of those things where you’re like, 'All right.'"
      

            Check out the clip ... he explained he tried to play it cool instead of run, but the boys still grabbed him, held him at knifepoint and asked for his money.
      
    
            Ben explained he was about to get out of it because he actually recognized who was mugging him.
      
    
            He said ... "I was scared. But then out of the corner of my eye, I realized who they were. I recognized them from playing baseball and they were like older boys that I knew and they were like, 'Oh yeah, what’s up?' And so I guess I was like, I guess I’m off the hook."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            But things didn't work out that way for another victim a few years later, Affleck revealed. He says the same kid who robbed him actually went on to kill someone else with a knife and went to prison for 20 years.
      
    
            Looks like Ben had quite the lucky break.

            Presley Gerber showed up high when he was admitted to the Resolutions Living sober house -- and he died just hours later -- but the doctor who owns Resolutions was in no mood to talk about it when we asked.
      
    
            We got Dr. Reza Nabavi in Malibu late Wednesday afternoon, and asked him about a story TMZ broke -- that Presley's sober coach called Resolutions and asked if Presley could stay in the facility's sober house, making it clear the son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber was high. We're told the admissions director said to bring him there. Multiple people in the rehab industry say there is a hard rule not to admit anyone into a sober house who is high.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The sober coach deposited Presley at the sober house and then left. We obtained video of Presley inside and he was clearly high. We're told he was doing drugs and apparently od'd hours later.
      

            Dr. Reza put his hand up to our photog and seemed indignant we asked about Presley and his admissions policies.
      
    
            As we reported, sources say the admissions director was fired and we're also told Dr. Reza has privately said the facility was not responsible, laying the blame on the sober coach.
